RQ-3: Check role/custody continuity and all practice meanings/keys, including reference of seu/sua and old-word story recall. Assess narrative substance.

grammar.title: Frase
grammar.rule: de + o → do; de + a → da. Meu livro; minha bolsa.

rows: Seu livro está na bolsa, Ana?

grammar.note_en:
De joins with definite articles just as em did in chapter 2: de + o becomes do, and de + a becomes da. O livro do irmão means “the brother’s book”; o envelope da dona means “the female owner’s envelope.” The article belongs to the following noun: irmão is masculine, dona feminine. The gender of the thing owned does not determine do/da. De before the personal names remains uncontracted in our register: de Rosa, de Paulo. Do not insert an article just to imitate the noun examples.

Meu/minha means “my”; seu/sua can mean “your,” “his” or “her,” depending on the speaker and context. These possessives agree with the thing or relation named, not the owner’s sex. Rosa is a woman but says O envelope é meu (“The envelope is mine”) because envelope is masculine. Ana says Minha bolsa é azul (“My bag is blue”) because bolsa is feminine. A foto é minha means “The photo is mine”: foto is feminine despite ending in o. Meu livro means “my book”; minha amiga means “my female friend.” The same forms can accompany the noun or stand after é when the noun is clear.

In direct speech, the named addressee resolves seu/sua: Rosa asks Ana A bolsa é sua? (“Is the bag yours?”); Ana says O livro na bolsa é do seu irmão (“The book in the bag belongs to your brother”), speaking to Rosa. In the phone message, Paulo? É Rosa, sua irmã means “Paulo? It is Rosa, your sister”: Rosa identifies herself to Paulo. Elsewhere, Rosa chama seu irmão means “Rosa calls her brother.” Do not translate every seu/sua as your automatically. When context would be unclear, a named phrase such as de Rosa states the relation explicitly.

Irmão and irmã mean “brother” and “sister”; amigo and amiga mean “male friend” and “female friend.” Paulo é meu irmão means “Paulo is my brother”; Rosa é irmã de Paulo means “Rosa is Paulo’s sister.” A sibling can also be a friend: these are not mutually exclusive categories. Dona/dono identifies an owner. Paulo é o dono do livro preto means “Paulo owns the black book”; Rosa é a dona do café means “Rosa owns the café.” Someone can hold an object without owning it.

De can also mark another association made clear by the scene: o livro da foto means “the book in the photo,” not a book owned by a photograph. A foto do irmão means “the photograph of the brother.” The image depicts Paulo, while Rosa has the photograph on her phone. In the table, de + o café → do café means “of the café”; de + a bolsa → da bolsa means “of the bag.” A pessoa na foto é o meu irmão means “The person in the photo is my brother”; A bolsa é sua means “The bag is yours.”

Pergunta means “asks,” responde “answers,” mostra “shows,” and sabe “knows.” They use the third-person singular forms with one named person. Ana pergunta Quem é a pessoa na foto? means “Ana asks who the person in the photo is”; Rosa responde É Paulo, meu irmão means “Rosa answers: It is Paulo, my brother.” Chama in the phone scene means “calls”: Rosa chama o irmão means “Rosa calls her brother.” A telephone number identifies the contact; the chapter never supplies Paulo’s reply or asserts that the bag has already been returned.

The remaining table examples translate as follows: Meu livro é branco means “My book is white”; Seu livro está na bolsa, Ana? means “Is your book in the bag, Ana?”; O envelope é seu, Rosa means “The envelope is yours, Rosa.” In the contractions table, de + o irmão → do irmão means “of the brother,” and de + a dona → da dona means “of the female owner.”
